limitations: All 67 PDF pages text-reviewed; three contact sheets cover all pages and 34 selected pages inspected at readable full-page size, including every hand-signal page. Not every page had a separate full-size inspection.
Cover PDF1 has an extracted zero but no visible printed label. PDF2–67 visibly use printed1–66, so printed=PDF minus1. No printed0 is invented.

No numbered source chapters. Ten disjoint editorial page containers include continuations: essential categories on PDF32, rally protocol on50 and cache continuation on59. Their editorial numbers are not book chapter labels. Exact item citations follow actual content.

Source title/byline Jack Maddox differs from metadata title HOW TO BECOME INVISIBLE IN THE OUTDOORS and author Diana Cule. Cause, authorship and Green Beret credentials are unauthenticated. No named publisher identified on title page.

Eight bag bullets, ten later essential categories, sixteen named hand signals and three radio-burst meanings are separately audited. Overlap between lists is retained, not counted as distinct purchases. Four face-paint steps, five ghost-walking steps and nine firearm-painting steps remain components of their parent methods.

Source photographs are visible-light illustrations, not tests of observer detection, thermal protection or field safety. Hand gestures were visually matched to nearby labels/text; no universal military/sign-language certification inferred.
No full procedure, project, concealed checkpoint passage, tracking countermeasure, cache system or thermal shield is verified. Narrow supported principles do not validate adjacent tactical claims.

No personal route, threat assessment, firearm configuration, clinical treatment, radio service/device compliance, land permission or cache deployment was assessed. Checkpoint content is summarized for review, not expanded into evasion instructions.

Some source cautions matter: environment-specific patterns, untreated clear water, firearm unloading/PPE/fire warnings, white-light first-aid exception, low-ground flood/cold warning and incomplete thermal concealment are retained.

EPA and CDC differ in published high-altitude boiling thresholds; this examination does not merge their numerical recipes or create a new treatment card. NPS cathole guidance is site-dependent, and CDC gives a different depth phrasing; do not average rules or ignore required pack-out.

DCR indexed official excerpt was reviewed but full page returned403. It is labeled primary_excerpt_reviewed and never supports a verified record. FCC guide and VDEM evacuation PDF also returned403; neither is used as reviewed evidence. An obsolete CDC emergency URL returned404; the working backcountry page was read instead.

VDH planning, DWR hunting visibility and a Virginia city route example constrain local application. Hunting requirements apply to specified activities; Virginia Beach routes are not assumed to be this household’s routes. DCR excerpt is not a complete personalized legal assessment.

USGS was considered for water/terrain questions but no hydrologic availability model or groundwater design is being verified; CDC/EPA address the actual treatment claims. No authority is attached merely to inflate evidence counts.

Household remains five people, no pets, public water/sewer and an irrigation well. Ages, mobility, medicines, route, season and destination unknown. No quantity, water yield, carry capacity or household readiness credit calculated.

record.title: Ten Essentials
record.finding: Outdoor essentials include navigation, extra clothing, illumination, first aid, nutrition, hydration and emergency shelter. Match the activity and conditions; the list is not a demonstrated 72-hour family capacity.

record.title: Outdoor Emergency Plan
record.locator: Before trip; group travel; lost response
record.finding: Practice equipment and the plan, use a mapped meeting location, stay together and use designated trails. If lost, assess safe retracing first; when seeking rescue, report location and stay unless immediately threatened. Visibility and signaling help rescuers.

record.title: Water Treatment Options When Hiking, Camping, or Traveling
record.finding: Clear streams may contain germs. Boiling targets germs; filtration and disinfection are not interchangeable. Follow product instructions, account for organism coverage and iodine contraindications. Chemical/toxin/radioactive contamination requires another source, not boiling or disinfection.

record.title: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water
record.finding: Flowing surface water is generally preferred to stagnant water, but still requires treatment. Boiling/disinfection do not eliminate metals, salts or most chemicals. Flooded wells need appropriate disinfection/testing. No site is certified potable by this page.

record.title: Resolve to be Ready for Emergencies
record.locator: Make a Resolution; Get Tech Ready
record.finding: Plan a safe meeting place, evacuation routes and an out-of-town contact. Maintain supplies and documents, receive local alerts and have device backup power. This is general planning, not a personalized route.

record.publisher: New Jersey Office of Emergency Management
record.title: Evacuation
record.locator: How do I evacuate; Go Kit; official alerts
record.finding: Official instructions inform evacuation routes, shelter and transport. A go kit must consider prescriptions, disabilities, childcare, identification and carrying capacity. Routes and transit arrangements are jurisdiction- and incident-specific.

record.title: Dispose of Waste Properly
record.finding: Check local rules and facilities. Some places require waste pack-out systems; where catholes are appropriate, NPS gives 6–8 inches and 200 feet from water, trails and camps. Pack out toilet paper. Concealment or generic double-bagging is not a complete sanitation plan.

record.title: The Skinny on Soap
record.locator: Soap impacts and distance from water
record.finding: Biodegradable soap still harms waters. Do not introduce soap into a stream or lake; wash away from water and minimize use. This constrains bathing/laundry, not proof of scent elimination.

record.title: Bear Safety: Storing Food
record.finding: Pack out scraps and garbage and treat attractants as food. Site-specific food-storage requirements may call for lockers or bear-resistant containers. Low odor, a resealable bag or a buried cache alone is not wildlife protection.

record.title: Novelty Makeup
record.finding: Use products intended for the skin and follow location-specific label warnings, especially around eyes. Contaminated products and irritation matter. Outdoor mud or arbitrary paint is not endorsed as face makeup.

record.title: Can Thermal Imaging See Through Walls?
record.finding: Typical thermal imagers observe surface radiation: ordinary walls, glass, metal and tree trunks do not offer direct see-through views; surfaces can warm or reflect. Smoke and darkness do not necessarily prevent imaging. This does not validate any personal concealment system.

record.title: Can Thermal Imaging See Through Fog and Rain?
record.finding: Range depends on detector band, atmosphere, target contrast and distance. Dense fog can limit infrared as severely as visible imaging; rain may significantly reduce contrast. No universal fog-penetration or safe-distance guarantee follows.

record.title: General Information & Hunting Regulations
record.finding: Blaze-color requirements apply to specified hunters and accompanying people, with season/activity exceptions. They are not a universal law for every hiker. Visibility and lawful land access must be assessed before adopting camouflage advice.

record.title: State Park Rules and Regulations
record.finding: Official indexed excerpt prohibits damaging or gathering park plants/materials outside limited permissions and says to use dumpsters or pack trash out. Full-page open returned 403; this excerpt is a constraint only, never verified support.

record.publisher: City of Virginia Beach Emergency Management
record.title: Evacuating
record.finding: Virginia Beach publishes designated hurricane routes and warns the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel is not one. Road and ramp controls illustrate why access changes need official local information. Do not use this city-specific page as this household’s actual route.

record.title: Stealth is not the default evacuation objective
record.guidance: Select routes, shelter and communications for the actual hazard. Do not hide from legitimate rescuers, substitute woods travel for official routes or assume strangers and checkpoints are hostile.

record.title: No camouflage performance guarantee
record.guidance: No controlled visual, acoustic, scent or thermal test establishes detection distance, reliability or protection for this family. Photographs demonstrate appearance, not adversarial effectiveness.

record.title: Clothing and equipment need practical suitability
record.guidance: Prioritize weather protection, fit, mobility, vision and necessary visibility. Material, color or military pedigree alone does not establish performance. Virginia hunting visibility rules have defined scopes and exceptions.

record.title: Skin products and mud are not interchangeable
record.guidance: Use a skin-intended product as labeled, with eye and irritation precautions. Do not infer mud is hygienic or that washing off is its only drawback. No camouflage efficacy follows from skin-product safety.

record.title: Firearm painting is not a readiness requirement
record.guidance: The book includes unloading, internal-parts, ventilation/PPE and flammability warnings; preserve those. It supplies no model-specific compatibility, respirator selection, coating safety or tested modification protocol. Seek manufacturer/qualified service guidance rather than execute this outline.

record.title: Departure kit is not demonstrated capacity
record.guidance: Tailor loads to each person, medical and accessibility needs, destination, season, transport and replenishment. Eight category bullets and ten essentials are not quantities, a complete five-person plan or proof of 72-hour survival.

record.title: Movement and trail choice need a safety plan
record.guidance: No universal silent gait, five-minute listening interval, ridgeline ban or off-trail route is validated. Avoid unnecessary falls, water hazards, separation and delay; practice within abilities and use designated routes where appropriate.

record.title: Vehicle abandonment needs incident-specific judgment
record.guidance: Congestion, increased activity or a checkpoint alone is not a sufficient reason to leave vehicle shelter, supplies and transport. Assess immediate danger, official instructions, accessibility and a reachable safe destination; no universal stay/leave rule is certified.

record.title: Natural-water clues are not a safety test
record.guidance: Animal tracks, vegetation, clear appearance or flowing water do not establish available, accessible potable water. EPA’s preference for flowing water is conditional on treatment. Do not substitute scent concealment for source assessment.

record.title: Match water treatment to hazards and product
record.guidance: Boiling addresses germs, not chemical hazards. Filters and tablets have different organism coverage, contact times and contraindications; follow actual product instructions. Do not turn a list of alternatives into equivalent complete purification.

record.title: Signals need explicit agreement and accessibility
record.guidance: The sixteen gestures are source examples, not a verified universal sign language. Check sightlines, darkness, ability and acknowledgment; do not replace urgent speech or emergency signaling with compulsory silence.

record.title: Checkpoint conduct is not an evasion guarantee
record.guidance: No appearance, timing or conversational technique establishes safe passage without inspection. Follow lawful emergency traffic controls and current route directions; do not bypass closures based on this book.

record.title: Radio clicks are not a reliable emergency protocol
record.guidance: Unspecified radios, squelch/tone settings, channel congestion, missed bursts and ambiguity are unresolved. Earpieces do not establish privacy or prevent radio detection. No FCC service compliance or device compatibility was validated; do not infer coded bursts are categorically lawful or unlawful.

record.title: Meeting plans should not create a second search
record.guidance: Agree on safe accessible locations, contacts and what to do if separated. A timed chain of concealed rally points may keep people moving past each other; children/dependents need an appropriate supervision plan. A lost-person response differs from a preplanned destination change.

record.title: Light must support safe travel and care
record.guidance: No universal white-light ban, filter-color guarantee or minimum brightness fits all tasks. Use enough light for footing, navigation and care, and preserve signaling when help is needed. The source explicitly permits white light for bleeding assessment.

record.title: Hygiene is not scent invisibility
record.guidance: Keep safe water, hand hygiene, foot/skin condition and drying practical. Unscented toiletries, daily powder or washing schedules are not proven anti-tracking measures. Avoid soap in natural water even if biodegradable.

record.title: No-cook planning differs from never cooking
record.guidance: Ready-to-eat food is useful, but no-cooking/no-fire rules are not universal survival rules. Food safety, weather, lawful fire restrictions and reliable water treatment take priority over odor suppression.

record.title: Waste disposal needs public-health and site controls
record.guidance: Use facilities or an approved pack-out method as required. Where permitted, follow site-specific cathole depth/location guidance and hand hygiene; deeper solely to hide odor is not a rule. Generic double bags do not establish leak control, disposal acceptance or drinking-water protection.

record.title: Pack trash and food waste out
record.guidance: Do not bury wrappers, scraps or other garbage to conceal them. Secure food and attractants under local wildlife rules. The page55 burial option conflicts with page56’s instruction to carry uneaten food; keep both source locations.

record.title: No track-erasure guarantee
record.guidance: Surface marks and disturbed plants may be observable, but no field trial establishes that stepping patterns, trail switching or faster movement defeats tracking. Do not destroy evidence, trespass or sacrifice safe travel to this unsupported promise.

record.title: Caches require permission and maintenance
record.guidance: No hidden cache is assumed legally placed, reliably retrievable, wildlife-proof, safe-temperature or potable. Get land permission, assess digging restrictions/utilities, contamination, access, shelf life and inspections. Do not rely on untested buried supplies as the only evacuation reserve.

record.title: Shelter safety comes before concealment
record.guidance: Use a lawful accessible site with protection from weather and ground hazards, suitable space and ventilation. Low tarp height, dense brush and rapid dispersal do not demonstrate safe five-person shelter. The book does warn that low ground can collect water and cold air.

record.title: Alarms and escape routes remain unvalidated
record.guidance: No early-warning-device design or tested response plan is supplied. Do not infer permission for traps or harmful devices. Avoid trip hazards and dependent separation; a sentry is not a substitute for a safe destination.

record.title: Thermal opacity is not invisibility
record.guidance: Material opacity at one sensor band or angle does not establish hidden occupancy. Surface warming, reflections, gaps, weather and other sensors matter; do not certify foil, glass, walls or trees as personal protection.

record.title: Weather does not have one thermal-camera result
record.guidance: Fog/rain effects depend on density, band, target and distance. The source already mentions reduced range, but blanket penetration language remains too broad; no evasion distance or day-versus-night rule is established.

record.title: Blankets, clothing and netting are not tested thermal shields
record.guidance: No instrumented test, duration, viewing geometry, wavelength or safety conditions support these specific assemblies. Preserve thermal comfort, ventilation and visibility to rescuers; the Taliban blanket anecdote is unauthenticated.

10 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• The colors in nature are not all the same, and the colors you wear and 
that make up your gear and camp should also not be all the same. 
Choose several different colors that will effectively blend into your 
environment and paint your equipment with a disruptive pattern using 
fabric paint. 
• Know how the changing seasons affect the color scheme of the 
environment that you are operating in. Plan accordingly and choose 
camouflage patterns that will cover all the seasons or have a few sets of 
equipment and clothing so that you can effectively blend in despite the 
time of year. The difference may be negligible in arid regions, but the 
environment could change from lush green to brown and then white 
through the seasons in temperate areas. 
Shape  
Certain shapes either do not exist in nature or exist so rarely that they become 
immediately apparent.  
One such example is anything with a right angle, and another immediately 
apparent shape is the human form.  
In each of these cases, to effectively disappear, we need to transform these 
obvious outlines into something that looks natural.  
A few steps that we can take to counteract our shape from being our betrayer 
are:

Shadow 
The problem with shadows is that when we hide behind an object, our shadow 
can be cast to the side, demonstrating to observers that someone is hiding 
there. However, using shadow to our advantage is possible and an essential 
aspect of becoming invisible in  the woods. In areas where there is a dark 
shadow cast, we can use these shadows to conceal ourselves further. This also 
applies to shadows cast by the moonlight as well. Even in the dark of night, 
there are areas that the light of the moon does not reach,  and these places can 
be fantastic places to find concealment. 
What we can do about the problem of shadows: 
• Make yourself aware of which direction the sun is shining and make sure 
that you will not cast a shadow in any direction that an observer may see. 
• If you are in an area for an extended period or are planning a permanent 
concealed position, keep a note of where shadows are cast and at which 
times. Use this knowledge to your advantage in planning the placement 
of your concealed positions. 
• Move from shadow to shadow and avoid the light at all costs when 
transiting areas. 
Silhouette  
Camouflage is effective as long as the background that we are blending into is 
similar to what we are wearing. If the sky is our background, then our disguise 
becomes useless.  
Avoiding silhouetting ourselves is something that the army drilled into us 
almost from day one. We can make few missteps regarding our camouflage that 
are as egregious and easily avoided as silhouetting ourselves.

16 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• Never walk along the top of a ridgeline. Instead, walk along the ridge at a 
point that is far enough below the crest where you will not find yourself 
silhouetted. Often this area is referred to as the military crest of a hill.  
• ALWAYS be aware of your background. Silhouetting does not always 
happen on a hilltop. If we walk within a treeline, the forest acts as an 
effective backdrop that conceals us, but the sky beyond the treeline 
serves to silhouette us to an observer within the forest. 
• If you must traverse a hill or ridge, either go around it or crawl over the 
top on your belly. 
Spacing  
Looking around any modern urban environment will show us that human 
beings like to space everything in an organized and even fashion. Nature, on the 
other hand, does not adhere to our need for organization. Much like shape, our 
eyes tend to be drawn to any spacing that looks artificial or 'man-made.' 
Fortunately, there are steps that we can take to avoid spacing being our 
downfall: 
• If you are placing several shelters in an area, randomize the spacing and 
orientation to avoid them catching the eye of someone observing the 
area. 
• The same is true for parking vehicles. Again, randomize the spacing and 
orientation of them to not look like a used car lot.

17 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• Use low ground (also referred to as 'dead ground') to conceal your 
movements. 
• Move under cover of darkness unless you are concerned about detection 
from thermal imaging or night vision. 
• Make all of your movements slow and deliberate avoid any sudden, 
violent, or jerky motions that may cause someone to take notice. 
Concluding Thoughts on ‘Why Things Are 
Seen’ 
To develop a good understanding of why things are seen, you must keep your 
eyes open to the world around you, noticing things that stand out and taking a 
second to think of why it is that you saw that object or person.  
If you want to be invisible in the outdoors, you need to begin by becoming very 
aware of your surroundings, and in turn, you will start to notice what is trying 
to avoid your detection.  
Being able to spot an animal, person, or object deliberately camouflaged is 
probably the most critical skill you should have to begin to make yourself 
invisible.

20 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
be superior to no camouflage, there is no reason that you cannot operate 
invisibly in the outdoors wearing only earth-toned colors. 
The key to successfully blending into the environment without a camouflage 
pattern is to match the colors of your clothing to the colors of the environment 
you find yourself in. Earth tones are best, and they should be of fabrics that are 
either natural or appear natural.  
Camouflaging Your Skin 
No matter how great your clothing blends into the background, your skin will 
stand out. Even if your skin tone is dark, your skin will still be shiny, and your 
face still looks like a human face. Therefore, we need to apply face paint to your 
face to create a pattern that will disrupt the telltale features of the human face 
while eliminating the natural shine. 
Our goal in camouflaging the face is to transform it into something that no 
longer looks human -like. The best way to accomplish this is to lighten areas 
often in shadows, like the hollows of the eyes and the ears, then darken raised 
areas, such as our forehead, 
nose, and jawline. 
You will have to experiment 
a bit to match your face paint 
to your operating 
environment. That being 
said, regardless of what 
pattern you are going to 
apply to your face, the steps 
for using the paint will be the 
same.

outline, less is more. There is no need to make ourselves look like a bush. We 
only need the shape of our body and equipment to appear no longer human -
like or artificial. 
Weapons And Gear 
The problem with firearms is, they have a distinct shape that looks like a 
firearm. They are also often manufactured in colors that stand out in the woods.  
Therefore, if you carry a gun with you as you disappear into the outdoors, paint 
it to blend in with your clothing and equipment's color scheme. Also, take 
measures to break up the weapon's outline to make it look less like a firearm.  
Painting a firearm can be done using readily available Earth tone spray paints 
with a flat finish. Several manufacturers of spray paint have product lines 
specifically for spray painting camouflage patterns. However, some paints are 
specifically designed for use on firearms, and these options usually require a lot 
more care and attention than spray paint. Of course, the trade -off is that the 
finish will last far longer. 
A few considerations that you need to take before painting a firearm will be: 
• Never paint internal components. These could become gummed up with 
paint causing malfunctions. 
• Use a variety of colors. 
• Always thoroughly clean and degrease the firearm before painting. 
• Mask any areas that you do not want to paint with painter's tape. 
• Wear a respirator and only paint in well-ventilated areas. 
• Use mesh, leaves, grass or other objects as stencils to create a unique 
camouflage pattern. 
• Use a light color as a base coat. Then, add the darker colors to create the 
pattern one at a time until you achieve the desired camouflage pattern. 
If you decide to paint your firearms, there are a few steps that you need to 
follow: 
1. Unload and clear the firearm. 
2. Disassemble the weapon and separate the parts you want to paint.

27 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
3. Clean the parts with a solvent and degreaser. Read and follow the 
manufacturer's instructions for the type of paint that you are using. In 
addition, there may be special cleaning and application instructions that 
you must follow. 
4. Prepare an area for painting, taking care to set up the space to eliminate 
the possibility of overspray getting on things that you don't want paint 
on. 
5. Wear the proper PPE and apply the first coat to the parts. Allow to dry 
and repeat the process until you are satisfied with the base coat. 
6. Use natural materials or mesh as a stencil and spray the next darker color. 
7. Repeat this process until you have sprayed all the colors you want on 
your weapon in the pattern you are happy with. 
8. Allow to dry and cure as per the manufacturer's directions. 
9. Reassemble the weapon, oil the internal components, and conduct a 
function test. 
Painting firearms will give you a massive advantage in your camouflage, but 
you can still up to your camo game by adding some materials such as pieces of 
a sniper's veil.  
The important thing to remember is that you do not want to add anything that 
will easily catch fire. The only places you should be placing additional 
camouflage are on the front handguard, the stock, and around the optics. 
Camouflaging Equipment 
Our equipment is also in need of camouflage. Fortunately, often we can 
purchase gear made from fabric that already has a camouflage pattern printed 
onto it. The problem is that all of this equipment still has a unique shape and 
could benefit from the addition of some natural camouflage. 
You could also tie or sew burlap strips to your gear, but this is not as effective 
as natural camouflage.

Finally, you must carry a means of communication or signaling, whether it is a

These items form the foundation of your ability to survive and operate 
effectively. Everything else is secondary. If you are forced to make decisions 
about what to carry, these essentials should always take priority. 
Move Like A Ghost 
Knowing how things are seen and effectively camouflage ourselves is only the 
first few steps in becoming invisible in the outdoors. If you want to stay hidden, 
then you need to move through the woods like a ghost. The way we do this is to 
move quietly and to listen carefully. 
Footwork 
How we step is the first and most crucial part of becoming a ghost in the 
wilderness. Our feet are the parts of our body that constantly touch the ground 
and, with every step, threatening to give away our position. Of course, you can 
choose footwear like m occasins that are soft -soled and, in turn, very stealthy, 
but with proper technique, you can walk very quietly regardless of your 
footwear choices. The primary technique that we want to use when moving 
silently through the woods is 'Ghost Walking.' How it works is that as we step, 
the foot is set on the ground carefully and deliberately rolling it into being flat 
on the ground.

34 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• Never crest a hill or ridge. Instead, move around the side to avoid 
silhouetting yourself. 
• Use creeks and streams to mask the sound of your movement. If your 
footfalls are being masked or not making a lot of noise, you can forego 
ghost-walking and walk at a quicker pace. 
• Use the low ground to avoid detection from observers, but periodically 
move to positions to get eyes on the high ground to potentially spot 
anyone who may observe you. 
• When you have to move in the open, stay as low as possible and 
minimize the amount of time you are exposed.  
• Move from cover to cover. 
Take The Road Less Traveled 
Humans are lazy by nature, and we like to take the easy path whenever we can. 
Any woodland area with a lot of human activity has a network of trails that 
follow the most accessible routes. Even animals like to follow the easy path and 
game trails are often the least difficult. While using well-travelled trails can be 
helpful to move rapidly, they also open us up to a significant amount of risk.  
To combat this, we can avoid any paths that appear to be well -travelled, but 
there are problems in doing this. The first being that the road less travelled is 
often less travelled for a reason. The terrain and vegetation may be too difficult 
to move quickl y, and the foliage may cause silent movement to be effectively 
impossible. 
A better solution is to use a hybrid of the two. For example, use the terrain that 
is not well travelled to conceal yourself and use the pathways that allow easy 
travel to move quickly through an area in short intervals.  
Only do so when you are sure that the odds of detection are low, and you can 
be alerted to people on the trail before they see you, giving yourself enough 
time to move off and let them pass. 
Avoid using game trails because they will attract hunters who will notice 
human tracks, alerting them to another person in the area.

There is a technique for stepping on and off the main trails. Take the largest, 
most exaggerated step off the path that you can. Pick an area with something 
that you can step behind that will hide any tracks that you may leave after you

step off, ensure the trail itself is not in such a state that it holds tracks well. The 
same is true of stepping onto the path.  
After you step off the trail, you should move parallel to the path for a way back 
along the way you came. Find an area to stop and observe the trail to make sure 
that you are not being followed. Also, before stepping onto a trail, conduct a 
five-minute listening halt to make sure the trail is clear. 
When to Abandon Your Vehicle 
In many emergency situations, a vehicle can help you cover ground quickly and 
carry more supplies than you could on foot. However, there comes a point 
where a vehicle becomes a liability rather than an advantage. Recognizing when 
to abandon your vehicle is  critical to maintaining mobility and avoiding 
detection. 
Vehicles are limited to roads and established paths. If those routes become 
blocked, monitored, or dangerous, staying with your vehicle may expose you to 
unnecessary risk. A stalled or disabled vehicle can also trap you in place and 
make you an easy target.

If time allows, take steps to reduce the likelihood that your vehicle will draw

Once on foot, your priorities shift to remaining undetected, conserving energy,

ability to move quietly and efficiently on foot will determine your chances of

Listening Halts 
Every so often, you should stop moving and spend at least five minutes 
listening to your surroundings. You and your group should be silent during 
this process. Once you are sure that the area is free of anything or anyone who 
may discover you, you can resume movement. 
Water Sources on the Move 
While moving through the outdoors, maintaining access to water is one of your 
highest priorities. Dehydration will quickly reduce your ability to think clearly, 
move efficiently, and remain aware of your surroundings. 
Finding water on the move requires understanding how water flows through the 
terrain. Low ground, valleys, and natural depressions are more likely to contain 
water than high ground. Streams and rivers are obvious sources, but smaller 
indicators such as damp soil, dense vegetation, or the presence of animal tracks 
can also lead you to water.

37 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Moving water is generally safer than stagnant water, but no natural source should 
be assumed safe without treatment. Even clear water can contain bacteria, 
parasites, or other contaminants that can cause serious illness. 
Because of this, you must always have a method of purification that is compact 
and easy to use while on the move. Boiling water is one of the most reliable 
methods, but it may not always be practical if you are trying to remain 
undetected. In these situations, filtration systems or purification tablets provide a 
faster and more discreet solution. 
When collecting water, minimize your exposure. Avoid spending unnecessary 
time at the source, especially in open areas where you may be visible. If possible, 
collect water quickly and move to a concealed location before treating and storing 
it. 
Water sources can also attract both animals and people, increasing the risk of 
detection. Always observe the area before approaching and remain alert while 
collecting water. 
Always carrying a small amount of water, along with a reliable purification 
method, allows you to stay mobile without depending entirely on known sources. 
The goal is to maintain a steady supply without slowing your movement or 
exposing your position. 
Communication 
If you are trying to disappear with a group, you will need to communicate 
amongst the group by speaking as little as possible. Fortunately, there are many 
ways that you can communicate in virtual silence with other group members.

46 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Communicating Through Voice 
If you must speak to a group member, only do so in a whisper through a cupped 
hand over the top of the person's ear. If the environment has a lot of background 
noise, such as running water, then you can exercise more freedom in 
communication through your voice.  
However, at all times, you should never speak above a whisper which should be 
quiet enough that it would be impossible to make out what you are saying from 
even a few meters away. 
How to Cross Checkpoints Without Getting 
Stopped 
In many situations, you may be forced to pass through controlled areas such as 
checkpoints, roadblocks, or zones where movement is being monitored. These 
locations are designed to identify threats, control movement, and gather 
information. Approaching them incorrectly can draw attention and put you at 
risk. 
The first rule when dealing with checkpoints is to avoid them whenever 
possible. If there is a safe alternative route, it is almost always better to use it. 
However, when avoidance is not an option, how you behave becomes critical. 
Your appearance should match the environment and the expectations of those 
controlling the checkpoint. Clothing, equipment, and overall presentation 
should not stand out or raise suspicion. Anything that looks out of place will 
draw attention. 
Movement and body language are just as important as appearance. You should 
move in a calm and deliberate manner, avoiding sudden movements or 
behavior that could be interpreted as nervous or evasive. Confidence without 
aggression is key.

47 
47 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Keep your actions simple and predictable. Do not volunteer unnecessary 
information and only respond to what is asked. The more you say, the more 
opportunities there are for inconsistencies or suspicion. 
Timing can also play a role. Moving during periods of higher activity may allow 
you to blend in more easily, while isolated movement can attract attention. 
Observing the checkpoint from a distance before approaching can provide 
valuable information about patterns, behavior, and potential risks. 
If you are carrying equipment, ensure that it is organized and does not appear 
threatening or unusual. Anything that draws attention may result in further 
inspection. 
The goal is not to deceive through complex actions, but to avoid standing out. 
Blending into the expected flow of people and maintaining controlled, natural 
behavior will reduce the likelihood of being stopped or questioned. 
Communicating Through Radio 
Using radio to communicate will become problematic since their use is almost 
entirely dependent on us using our voices to speak into the radio. In addition, 
speakers on radios can be loud as well, which will give your position away.  
One way to combat the speaker giving away your position is to use earpieces 
instead of the built -in speakers. Most of these earpieces will also include a 
microphone so that you can position close to your mouth.

48 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
In situations where you do not want to speak into the radio, you can instead key 
the push to talk button momentarily, which will cause the other radios on the 
same frequency to break squelch briefly. You can designate a meaning based on 
the number of times the squelch is broken in a row.  
As an example: 
Break Squelch Three Times = Meet at the rendezvous 
Break Squelch Twice = Approaching camp 
Break Squelch Once = Danger or stay still 
Keep the volume at the lowest level that allows for effective communication, 
and make sure that the LED display will not illuminate when you are 
transmitting. 
Rally Point Protocol 
If you are moving with a group or your family, there is always the possibility 
that you may become separated. In a high -stress situation, confusion, terrain, 
and limited visibility can quickly split even well -organized groups apart. 
Without a plan, this can lead to panic and poor decision-making. 
A rally point protocol ensures that separated individuals can regroup without 
needing to rely on communication devices that may fail or give away your 
position. 
Before moving into any area, you should establish at least one primary rally 
point and one or more secondary rally points. These locations should be easy 
to identify but not obvious to others who may be in the area. 
A good rally point should be easy for your group to recognize, while also being 
located away from roads, trails, and other high -traffic areas. It needs to be 
defensible and provide adequate concealment, and it should be accessible from 
multiple directions to allow flexibility in movement. 
In addition to choosing the location, you must also establish timing. Decide how 
long each person should wait at the rally point before moving on to the next

one. This prevents people from waiting too long in one place and risking 
detection. 
If radios are available, simple signals can be used to coordinate movement. For 
example: 
Break squelch three times = Move to the rally point 
However, you should never rely entirely on communication devices. A 
predetermined plan is far more reliable. 
Each member of the group must understand the plan fully. If even one person 
is unsure of the rally points or timing, the system can fail. 
The goal is simple: if you become separated, there is no confusion about where 
to go or what to do. Everyone follows the same plan, and the group comes back 
together without unnecessary risk. 
Light Discipline 
During the nighttime hours, it is imperative to keep your use of artificial light 
to a minimum. Sometimes this may be unavoidable, especially when you need 
to do tasks like consulting a map. However, there are a few rules for the use of 
light in situations where your goal is to remain undetected: 
• Avoid the use of white light at all costs. Have a red and blue color filter 
for your flashlight and headlamps. You want two colors of filters because 
under a red filter, the color red will not be visible, and likewise, under a 
blue filter, the color blue will not show up. Switch these filters depending

Mind The Wind 
Any hunter will tell you that the wind is one of the driving factors preventing 
your prey from detecting you. The same can be said for any people who may be 
looking to locate you. The problem is that you cannot control where the wind 
blows, and while you will want to move into the wind so that anyone ahead of 
you will not smell you, anyone following you will be treated to whatever funky 
odors you've managed to generate.  
No Cooking 
If you want to be invisible, you cannot cook food. The act of even warming 
food up will cause the odors of that food to be carried along with the breeze 
towards people that you potentially do not want to discover you and your 
camp. So instead, eat food that requires no preparation and is wrapped in 
packaging that you can open quietly. 
Bury Your Human Waste  
We all have to void our bowels as a course of daily living. As we try to be 
invisible in the woods, we need to bury that waste deep enough to eliminate the 
smell, and there is no possibility of our makeshift toilet being discovered. 
Leaving No Trace 
If someone is actively tracking you, take steps to ensure that you leave as close 
to zero traces of your presence as possible. Doing this will be very challenging 
and require a significant amount of discipline to pull off.

distance, then step off the path by 
taking a giant step in such a way that anyone who is tracking you will

55 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Covering Our Tracks 
Covering our tracks rarely works as well as we intend. What we see in the 
movies in the way of brushing our tracks away with a leafy branch or trying to 
walk backwards are methods that may fool inexperienced trackers. However, 
anyone who is knowledgeable and experienced in the art of tracking will not 
be fooled. It is better to make an effort to leave as few tracks as possible than 
to try and erase any tracks that you do leave. Depending on who is tracking 
you, it may be a better strategy to move faster than those who are in pursuit 
rather than make attempts to trick them.  
Garbage 
Do not leave any trash behind. It sounds simple and an obvious aspect of being 
invisible in the outdoors, but the issue is, policing your garbage is a lot more 
complicated than we would suspect.  
Every wrapper, piece of paper, human excrement, shell casing, and uneaten 
food must be accounted for and 
either carried with you or buried 
deep enough that there is no 
possibility of it being uncovered 
accidentally. 
One way trash can be accidentally 
left behind is when a wrapper or 
other bits of debris is inside your 
pocket. As your hand moves in and 
out of the pocket, there is always the 
probability of a piece of rubbish falling from the pocket onto the ground without 
you noticing it.  
The best way to combat this is to carry a ziplock bag in which you place all the 
trash you produce. A bag of that size is far more challenging to lose accidentally 
than a crumpled-up gum wrapper.

Foodstuffs 
In any survival or off -grid scenario, you should be leaving no food uneaten. 
However, if you find yourself with portions of food that have not been 
consumed, do not discard them into the bush or attempt to bury them. Instead, 
carry them with you in the sam e way that you transport your food. This 
includes the packaging of the food as well.  
Human Waste 
Human excrement will be a big sign that you are in an area because you cannot 
stop yourself from voiding your bowels. Even urine can lead to your detection 
if it is fresh enough where the odor is still hanging in the air, or the liquid is 
pooled on the ground or has made the vegetation or soil wet. The best way to 
avoid having your bowel movements give away your location is to carry them 
with you double bagged. However, this is an extreme measure and not one that 
everyone will want or need to do. The alternative is to bury your waste deep 
enough that it will not be discovered, and i n such a way, there is little to no 
evidence that the ground was disturbed. 
Shell Casings 
Depending on the situation, you may find yourself having to discharge a 
firearm. You must retrieve the shell casing for every round of ammunition you 
expend if you want to stay as invisible as possible.

57 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• Choose a shelter site and sleeping area that will result in minimal 
disruption in the ground, leaving as little sign as possible that someone 
slept there. 
• Do not build a fire. Not only does a fire betray you through the light and 
smoke it produces but erasing the existence of a fire pit from the ground 
is almost impossible. 
• Move around the area as little as possible. Every step that you take leaves 
sign. 
Supply Cache Strategy 
If you are forced to move over long distances, carrying everything you need on 
your back is not always practical. Weight slows you down, increases fatigue, 
and makes it harder to remain undetected. 
A supply cache strategy allows you to pre-position essential supplies along your 
route so that you can travel lighter while still having access to critical resources 
when needed. 
A cache is simply a hidden store of supplies placed in advance. These can 
include food, water, clothing, medical supplies, or equipment that you may need 
later. 
When selecting a cache location, you should choose an area that is difficult to 
stumble upon accidentally, easy for you to relocate using terrain features, away 
from common travel routes, and protected from the elements. 
Caches should be concealed carefully. Burying them is one option, but you must 
take care to leave minimal disturbance to the ground. Another option is to hide 
supplies under natural cover such as logs, rocks, or dense vegetation. 
Waterproof containers should always be used to protect the contents from 
moisture and environmental damage.

58 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
It is also important to avoid placing all your supplies in a single location. 
Multiple smaller caches reduce the risk of losing everything if one is discovered. 
When using a cache, approach the area carefully and observe it from a distance

approach it. 
A well-planned cache system allows you to move faster, carry less weight, and 
extend your operational range without sacrificing essential supplies. 
Invisible Shelter Options 
No matter the tactical situation, we will need some form of shelter to protect 
ourselves from the elements. Unfortunately, good shelter sites can be hard to 
find when you are not trying to be invisible, so when you want to shelter 
undetected, you are more than likely to have to settle for shelter sites that are 
less than desirable. 
Site Selection 
The key here is to select a shelter location that no one is going to stumble upon 
accidentally. This means that it has to be far removed from any populated areas, 
roads, paths, or game trails. Beyond that, you will also want to enter and exit

59 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
from the shelter site at points that are not visible from anyone who would care 
to notice. 
The best practice would be to have a significant amount of brush and shrub 
between yourself and anyone who would be looking for you. Along with this, 
you could choose a shelter site that is overly difficult to access or that has entry 
and exit points that you can camouflage effectively.  
One example would be to have shrubs or brush that you could place at the 
entrances and exits, which can quickly move out of the way.  
Alternatively, you could select an area that you could enter and exit from that 
has vegetation that appears to be challenging to negotiate but that you and your 
group members can slip through relatively quickly. 
Entry And Exit Points 
Never use the same point to both enter and exit the shelter site. If you are being 
pursued, the highest likelihood of your shelter being discovered is through the 
point that you enter it.  
Therefore, this point should be as concealed as practical and observable from 
the shelter site. The best-case scenario is to place a few early warning devices 
at this point so that if your site is compromised, you can make a hasty exit. 
As for exit points, you should never rely on only one. Instead, there must be 
several exit routes so that you and your group members can escape in seconds 
through different ways, rendezvousing later at a predetermined point.

Staying Aware 
If you are hiding in the woods, you are on the defensive and, in turn, need to 
think about how you are going to spot someone approaching your shelter 
before they spot you. The best way to do this is to use early warning devices, 
but posting a sentry is also good practice when more than one person is hiding 
in the woods. Regardless of how you will be warned of impending danger, you 
also should be orienting your shelter to have a view of the most likely avenues 
of ingress by people you are trying to be invisible from. 
Hiding From Thermal Vision 
Devices 
One of the most difficult methods of detection to hide from are thermal imagers. 
These devices are used in helicopters and drones, can be mounted on vehicles, 
and have become small enough to be portable and easy to deploy in a wide 
variety of locations. Thermal imaging is typically used by the military and law 
enforcement but has found its way into the civilian market in recent years. 
Defeating thermal imaging is very difficult and unfortunately cannot be done in 
such a way as to conceal oneself fully. Still, we can mask our infrared signature 
enough to limit any observer's ability to pick our signature out of the 
background. 
How Does Thermal Imaging Work? 
A thermal imager detects the infrared radiation that everything above zero 
degrees Kelvin emits. Once the camera detects the infrared radiation, it 
translates it into an image demonstrating the difference in temperature 
between the objects in the camera's field of view. The imager can display a 
colorized image or a black and white image depending on the type and purpose 
of the unit.

Best Practices For Avoiding Detection By 
Thermal Vision Devices 
While there are things that you can do to hide from thermal vision, there are 
also a few things that you should do first to avoid detection from thermal 
imagers. If you suspect that there are areas under surveillance through thermal 
vision, you should avoi d those areas as the first line of defense. If you cannot 
avoid areas that may be under surveillance by thermal imaging or if you are 
attempting to evade drones, there are a few things that you can do to reduce 
your odds of being discovered. 
• Thermal imaging cannot see through tree trunks, but it can be used to 
pick out heat signatures within forested areas. When moving through 
forested areas, stay close to the trunks of trees and move from cover to 
cover swiftly. Avoid treelines and open spaces, and when you find places 
that offer concealment, exploit them to your fullest advantage.  
• Avoid moving at night when there is a threat of detection from thermal 
imaging. Instead, move during the daylight hours when there will be 
many more heat signatures to blend with.  
• Only move when necessary. Staying still undercover will keep you hidden 
far better than if you decide to move from place to place.

64 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
How To Shield Yourself From Detection By 
Thermal Imaging 
There are not a lot of good options for shielding oneself from thermal cameras. 
However, we can try and block or diffuse our heat signatures in the hopes that 
it will make our heat signatures more challenging to spot.  
Blocking Infrared 
There are a couple of ways to block infrared radiation that are field expedient.  
The first is to build a shelter that has thick walls and overhead cover. The 
walls will help to mask your signature, and the overhead cover will diffuse the 
radiation that leaks from the shelter. This is an excellent option for a 
permanent shelter setup or a semi-permanent shelter but not a good option if 
you will be on the move.  
Mylar emergency blankets can be used to block the heat that our body emits 
and should be used to line a shelter or to cover ourselves. The big problem with 
mylar blankets is that they are shiny or colored with bright colors. Some styles 
are green in color, and these would be better to use.

Wool blankets can also be used to cover oneself with or use as overhead cover 
for your shelter. Using heavy wool blankets is a strategy that the Taliban have 
used to avoid detection by thermal imaging by Allied forces 
Wear insulated clothing to keep the heat from escaping into the surrounding 
air. Your exposed skin will still show up on thermal imagers, but your body will 
be less noticeable. 
Diffusing Infrared 
When blocking infrared is not possible or practical, you can take some 
measures to diffuse your heat signature. 
Camouflage netting will still allow infrared radiation to escape through the 
holes but block enough of it to lessen your overall heat signature. 
Ghillie suits also diffuse your heat signature.
